Advanced cancer patients often experience poor symptom control and medication adherence, with limited access to organized home-based palliative care (HBPC) in Egypt.
This study evaluated the impact of a structured HBPC program on patients' quality of life, symptom management, and medication adherence.
A quasi-experimental pre-post study was conducted at the National Cancer Institute in Cairo with a purposive sample of 10 patients.

Post-intervention analysis revealed a highly significant improvement (P < 0.001) in symptom severity (ESAS), overall palliative care outcomes (POS), and medication adherence (MMAS-8), with mean adherence scores increasing from 4.2 \pm 1.2 to 7.1 \pm 0.9.
A structured home-based palliative care program is effective in reducing symptom burden, enhancing quality of life, and improving medication adherence.
Integrating structured HBPC models into oncology nursing protocols and specialized staff training are essential to optimize patient outcomes.

Although advancements in cancer treatment have allowed patients with advanced- stage disease to live longer, they continue to face significant challenges, including inadequate symptom control and difficulties with medication adherence. Patients often require hospitalization to manage cancer-related symptoms and carry out daily activities, an experience that is frequently unpleasant. Furthermore, non-adherence to medication remains a critical issue in palliative care, with consequences that include poor health outcomes, recurrent hospital admissions, increased morbidity, and medication waste. Psychological distress and adverse side effects are primary factors that negatively influence this adherence to treatment

Table (2) shows frequency and percentage regarding the Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS) among the studied patients (pre and post).

The results showed great improvement in all ESAS symptom items after implementation of the structured home-based palliative care program. Severe pain decreased from 60% pre-intervention to 10% post-intervention. Severe fatigue also declined from 60% to 10%, while severe nausea decreased from 50% to 10%.

Regarding psychological symptoms, severe depression decreased from 50% to 10%, and severe anxiety decreased from 50% to 10%. Additionally, poor well-being showed the highest pre-intervention severity (70%), which markedly improved post-intervention, with only 10% remaining in the severe category.
These findings indicate that the home-based palliative care program had a positive effect on reducing physical and psychological symptom burden among patients with advanced cancer.

From the researchers’ perspective, the predominance of female patients may be attributed to the inclusion of breast cancer cases, which represented the highest proportion among the studied sample. The higher percentage of patients aged more than 45 years may be related to the increased incidence of advanced cancer among older adults. Furthermore, the high proportion of married patients and those living with family may reflect the importance of family support in caring for patients with advanced cancer, which facilitates participation in home-based palliative care programs. The predominance of urban residents may be explained by easier access to healthcare services and follow-up facilities available in urban areas compared to rural regions. From the researchers’ perspective, the marked improvement in medication adherence may be attributed to the educational and supportive components of the structured home-based palliative care program. Regular follow-up, medication counseling, and continuous communication through the smartphone application may have increased patients’ awareness of the importance of adhering to prescribed medications and helped them overcome barriers such as forgetfulness and misunderstanding of treatment instructions. In addition, family involvement and support within the home setting may have played an important role in reminding patients to take their medications as prescribed, thereby enhancing overall adherence levels.

The present study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. The small sample size may limit the generalizability of the results to a wider population of patients with advanced cancer receiving palliative care. In addition, the study was conducted in a single setting, which may reduce the applicability of the findings

The short follow-up period may not be sufficient to evaluate the long-term sustainability of improvements in symptom burden, quality of life, and medication adherence. Moreover, the use of self-reported tools such as ESAS, POS, and MMAS-8 may introduce recall and social desirability bias, potentially overestimating the observed improvements. Finally, although an application was initially planned to support the intervention, it was not effectively
utilized, which may have limited additional benefits in patient monitoring and communication.
